query: Which method can be used for reduce the sintering temperature, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using spark plasma sintering (SPS) enables densification of mechanically alloyed high-entropy alloy powders at a lower sintering temperature than conventional sintering methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Mechanically alloyed HEA powders having high surface area and reactive interfaces.
generation.intervention: Apply spark plasma sintering (SPS) with a pulsed electric current under moderate pressure and protective atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Inert atmosphere with controlled pressure; sintering temperatures around 1200°C or lower, with rapid heating/cooling cycles typical of SPS.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced localized Joule heating at particle contacts, which promotes rapid neck formation and diffusion across particles.
generation.mechanism: The pulsed current in SPS generates localized high-energy sites at particle interfaces, accelerating mass transport and reducing reaction times. This results in effective densification at lower temperatures by minimizing grain growth and reducing the energy barrier for diffusion compared to conventional furnace sintering.
generation.predicted_outcome: SPS-processed HEA samples will achieve near-full density and refined microstructures at lower sintering temperatures compared to those processed by traditional sintering methods.
generation.baseline: Traditional sintering or vacuum arc-melting methods require higher temperatures and longer dwell times to achieve similar densification, often at the expense of grain coarsening or oxidation.
generation.boundary: This approach is effective when powders are electrically conductive and form well-connected necks; its benefit may be less pronounced in systems with poor powder conductivity or where oxidation control is inadequate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of temperature reduction and the microstructural refinement achieved can vary with alloy composition, powder size, and specific SPS parameters and may require process optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA powder compacts under identical conditions. Process one set using conventional furnace sintering at a standard high temperature and the other using SPS at a lower temperature. Ensure both are conducted under comparable pressure and protective atmosphere. Evaluate densification, grain structure, and phase composition.
measurements: SEM imaging to assess microstructure and grain size
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If SPS-processed samples do not achieve comparable or improved densification and microstructural refinement at a significantly lower temperature than conventionally sintered samples, then the hypothesis that SPS reduces the effective sintering temperature would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: According to the traditional alloy design theory, ordered phases or intermetallic compounds will form as the number of alloying elements increases. However, Yeh et al. observes that simple solid solution phases, instead of intermetallic compounds, are formed in an equiatomic quinary alloy. Subsequently, they propose a new alloy system, termed high entropy alloys (HEAs), which contain at least five principal elements, each having the atomic percentage between 5% and 35% [ [1] , [2] ]. Since the development of HEAs, a substantial number of studies on HEA have been performed. Some of these studies are focused on alloys comprised of elements with low melting points, such as AlCoCrCuFeNi system alloys [ [3] , [4] ], commonly exhibiting high ductility and low strength. On the other hand, refractory HEAs have exhibited advantages of high yield strength at room and elevated temperature. MoNbTaTiW RHEA with an equimolar ratio of the elements was prepared by spark plasma sintering. Commercially available Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and W elemental powders were used as raw materials. The purity of all the powders was higher than 99.5%. The particle size of Mo, Nb, Ta, and Ti were less than 38 µm and that of W was less than 5 µm. After being proportioned in an equal molar ratio, the powders were mixed by planetary ball milling for 6 h. The mixed powders were put into a graphite mold and sintered in a spark plasma sintering furnace by vacuum hot pressing. The sintering temperature was 1500 °C, the pressure was 30 MPa, and the holding time was 20 min. The as-prepared MoNbTaTiW RHEA was used as the substrates. The MoNbTaTiW RHEA was cut into 5 mm × 5 mm × 20 mm cuboids whose surfaces were polished using 2000 mesh sandpaper and cleaned with acetone.

A Si-20Cr-20Fe (wt.%) coating was prepared on the RHEA cuboids by a fused slurry method. The particle size of Si powder was less than 10 µm, and that of Cr powder and Fe powder was less than 76 µm.
